title: Jeremiah 32:36–44
context: Jeremiah 32:36–44 continues the LORD’s answer, now turning to hope for the same city the people say is lost. He will gather his people from every land where he drove them, bring them back, and let them live safely. They will be his people and he will be their God. He will give them one heart and one way so they fear him forever, make an everlasting covenant not to turn away from doing them good, and put his fear in their hearts so they will not depart from him. As he brought disaster, he will bring all the good he promised, and fields will again be bought and deeds signed across the land, because he will reverse their captivity. The promise of a new heart echoes Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 (with 30:6) and stands close to the new covenant of 31:31–34, which Hebrews 8 quotes. Questions about whether God’s people persevere to the end are discussed at 1 Samuel 12:22; this unit shares that ground without opening a new divide.

verses.text: Now therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says concerning this city, about which you say, “It is given into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence:”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD now speaks about the city the people say is given to Babylon by sword, famine, and pestilence. Arminians see God turning from judgment to promise, addressing the people’s despair directly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the word now therefore as marking a turn to God’s purpose of restoration. Both traditions read the verse as taking up the people’s own words in order to answer them with hope.

verses.text: “Behold, I will gather them out of all the countries where I have driven them in my anger, and in my wrath, and in great indignation; and I will bring them again to this place. I will cause them to dwell safely.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will gather them from all the lands where he drove them in anger and bring them back to live safely. Arminian readers see God’s mercy following judgment, as he promised in the covenant (compare Deuteronomy 30:3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness to restore his people. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note that the return from exile was a first step toward fulfilling this promise.

verses.text: Then they will be my people, and I will be their God.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will be his people and he will be their God. Arminians see the heart of the covenant relationship, which God promises to restore after the exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the covenant formula repeated throughout Scripture (compare 31:33). Both traditions hold this as shared ground about God’s purpose to dwell with his people.

verses.text: I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their good and the good of their children after them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will give them one heart and one way, so they fear him forever for their good and their children’s. Arminian readers see God’s grace renewing the heart and enabling a faithful response, while still calling people to walk in that way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s grace as giving a new heart that surely produces fear of him. Both traditions point to Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 (with 30:6), where the same longing for a faithful heart is discussed, and they do not open a new divide here.

verses.text: I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from following them, to do them good. I will put my fear in their hearts, that they may not depart from me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises an everlasting covenant: he will not turn away from doing them good and will put his fear in their hearts so they will not depart. Arminians read the promise as God’s faithful commitment to his people, with the inward fear he gives sustaining them as they continue to trust him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see here God’s guarantee that his people will persevere because he keeps them. Whether God’s people persevere to the end is discussed at 1 Samuel 12:22, and both traditions note the close link with the new covenant of 31:31–34 and Hebrews 8:10.

verses.text: Yes, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will rejoice over them to do them good and plant them in the land with his whole heart and soul. Arminian readers see God’s delight in blessing his people, which shows that his heart is for their good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the language as expressing God’s full commitment to his promise. Both traditions note how unusual it is for God to speak of his whole heart and soul, and they read it as emphasizing the certainty of his good purposes.

verses.text: For the LORD says: “Just as I have brought all this great evil on this people, so I will bring on them all the good that I have promised them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that as he brought this great evil on the people, so he will bring all the good he promised. Arminians see God’s faithfulness in both judgment and blessing, so that his promises of good are as reliable as his warnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over both disaster and restoration. Both traditions read the verse as answering Jeremiah’s question: the same God who fulfilled his warning will fulfill his promise.

verses.text: Fields will be bought in this land, about which you say, ‘It is desolate, without man or animal. It is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says fields will be bought in the land the people call desolate and handed to the Chaldeans. Arminian readers see the sign of Jeremiah’s purchase explained, since what he did will one day be done by many.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s promise reversing the people’s despair. Both traditions note that the verse repeats the people’s own words, It is desolate, in order to answer them.

verses.text: Men will buy fields for money, sign the deeds, seal them, and call witnesses, in the land of Benjamin, and in the places around Jerusalem, in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the lowland, and in the cities of the South; for I will cause their captivity to be reversed,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says people will buy fields and sign deeds throughout Benjamin, Jerusalem, and Judah, because he will reverse their captivity. Arminians see the promise extending to every region, showing that restoration will be complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the detailed list of regions as underlining God’s faithfulness. Both traditions read the verse as completing the explanation of the sign at Anathoth in Benjamin, where the unit began.
